posts.headline: The Fed raised rates and nobody noticed
posts.caption:
Everyone is waiting for rate cuts. In September the Fed went the other way.

The target range is 3.75% to 4.00%.
That was a quarter-point increase, not a cut.
It has not moved since.

My take: the story people repeat and the number on the page stopped matching months ago.

Did you think rates were coming down this year?

Source: Federal Reserve, Sept 17 2026

posts.headline: What one point on a mortgage really costs
posts.caption:
One percentage point sounds small. Run it on a real loan.

$400,000 at 7.03% is about $2,669 a month.
The same loan at 6.03% is about $2,406.
That gap is $263 a month.

Over thirty years it is roughly $94,800 — a second deposit, paid to the bank instead.

My take: people shop the house for months and the rate for an afternoon.

Would one point change what you could buy?

Source: Forbes Advisor, Nov 9 2026

posts.headline: Same debt, two speeds
posts.caption:
A $5,000 card balance at 22%. The only difference is what you pay each month.

$150 a month clears it in 4 years 4 months, and costs $2,798 in interest.
$300 a month clears it in 1 year 9 months, and costs $1,022.

Same debt. Same rate. $1,776 difference.

My take: the card company sets the minimum. Everything above it is yours to decide.

Which number is closer to what you pay now?

Source: calculated at 22% APR

posts.headline: The same $200 a month, started later
posts.caption:
$200 a month until 65. The only thing that changes is when you start.

Start at 25: about $525,000.
Start at 35: about $244,000.
Start at 45: about $104,000.

Ten years of delay costs more than the next twenty years of saving.

My take: the money you put in barely changes. Time does all the work.

posts.headline: APR and APY are not the same word
posts.source: Source: Truth in Savings Act definitions
posts.caption:
Two letters apart. They sit on opposite sides of your money.

APR is what you are charged when you borrow.
APY is what you are paid when you save.
APY includes compounding. APR usually does not.

A bank will quote you whichever one looks better.

My take: read which letter is on the page before you read the number.

Do you know the APY on your own savings account?

Source: Truth in Savings Act definitions
Educational only — not financial advice.

#Banking #Savings #PersonalFinance

data.dek: One is what you pay. One is what you earn. Banks quote whichever flatters them.

posts.headline: What a one percent fee takes
posts.caption:
A 1% fee does not sound like a lot. Give it thirty years.

$100,000 growing at 7% becomes about $761,000.
The same money at 6% becomes about $574,000.
The one point difference is roughly $187,000.

My take: nobody sends you a bill for this. It just quietly isn't there at the end.

Do you know what your retirement account charges you?

Source: calculated on $100,000 over 30 years
Educational only — not financial advice.

posts.headline: How one late payment keeps costing you
posts.caption:
The late fee is the cheapest part.

A payment lands 30 days late.
It goes on your credit file and can sit there seven years.
A lower score raises the rate on the next loan you take.

The fee was $35. The score is what costs you.

My take: autopay the minimum on everything, then pay properly on top. The minimum is insurance, not a plan.

Is every card you own on autopay right now?

Source: FICO scoring factors
Educational only — not financial advice.

posts.headline: Clear the debt or build the cushion
posts.caption:
You have $1,000 spare. Two honest answers.

Paying down a 22% card is a guaranteed 22% return.
No savings account pays close to that.
But a card you have paid off is also a card you can run up again when the car breaks.

My take: a small cushion first, then attack the card. The cushion is what stops the card coming back.

Which would you do with $1,000 today?

Source: calculated, 22% APR against 4% APY
Educational only — not financial advice.

posts.headline: What $10,000 does if you leave it alone
posts.caption:
$10,000. No more added. Thirty years.

Year 10: about $19,700.
Year 20: about $38,700.
Year 30: about $76,100.

The first double takes ten years. The last double takes ten years and adds $38,000.

My take: the boring middle is where it happens, and it is also where most people sell.

What is the longest you have left money untouched?

Source: calculated at 7% a year
